chapter_summary:
SD cards can fail, become corrupted, or be accidentally overwritten. A reliable backup strategy is essential for any serious Raspberry Pi project. There are two main approaches: full image backups and file-level backups.

A full image backup creates a copy of the entire SD card. You can use Raspberry Pi Imager to read the card back to an image file on your computer. On Linux or macOS, you can also use the `dd` command:

```bash
sudo dd if=/dev/sdX of=backup.img bs=4M status=progress
```

Replace `/dev/sdX` with the device path of your SD card. Be extremely careful with `dd`; writing to the wrong device can destroy data. To restore the image to a new card:

```bash
sudo dd if=backup.img of=/dev/sdX bs=4M status=progress
```

For regular file-level backups, `rsync` is efficient because it only copies files that have changed. You can back up your home directory to an external drive or another computer:

```bash
rsync -avz --delete /home/alex/ /mnt/backup/pi_home/
```

The `--delete` option removes files from the backup that no longer exist on the source, keeping the backup in sync.

You can also create backups over the network:

```bash
rsync -avz /home/alex/projects/ alex@backupserver:/backups/pi/
```

For projects that change frequently, consider automating backups with a `cron` job that runs every night. Store important configuration files, scripts, and data in version control with Git so you can track changes and collaborate.

Disaster recovery also means documenting your project. A good README file should include:

- Project description and goals
- Hardware list with part numbers
- Wiring diagram or photos
- Software dependencies and installation steps
- How to run the project
- How to back up and restore

screens.title: Backups, Imaging, and Disaster Recovery
screens.subtitle: Keep your Raspberry Pi projects recoverable with full images, file backups, and good documentation

narration.text: In this lesson we will build a simple, reliable habit for protecting Raspberry Pi projects. You will learn two complementary backup strategies: full SD card imaging and file-level backups with a tool named rsync. Imaging captures everything on the card so you can restore a complete system, while rsync efficiently copies only changed files. We’ll also discuss safe use of low-level tools, automating backups to run overnight, and the single most overlooked item: clear documentation so someone else — or you months from now — can rebuild the project. A strong backup plan mixes an image for disaster recovery, regular rsync snapshots for day-to-day changes, and a README listing hardware, wiring, and install steps. As you go through the examples on the next screens, watch for common mistakes: writing a backup to the wrong device, trusting a single copy, or missing configuration files in version control. By the end you’ll be able to create an image, restore it, script rsync jobs, and describe how to recover your project. What would you want to find first after a card failure?

narration.text: These four objectives focus your practical skills for keeping a Raspberry Pi project recoverable. First, you will learn to create a full SD card image and understand when that is the right tool: to snapshot an entire system including the operating system, installed packages, and configuration. Second, you will practice restoring an SD card from an image so you can quickly recover to a known good state after a failure. Third, you will use rsync to perform incremental file backups and synchronize directories; this skill saves time and bandwidth for daily changes. Finally, you will document a project with a README that lists hardware, wiring, and install steps so a future restore is repeatable. Each objective includes a small visual cue or mnemonic to help you remember the distinction between complete images, file-level backups, automation, and documentation. Achieving these objectives reduces downtime and helps you recover from corruption, accidental overwrite, or card failure with clear steps to follow.

screens.title: Why backups matter for Raspberry Pi projects
screens.subtitle: Understand failure modes and choose the right backup strategy

narration.text: Backups start with understanding how things fail. SD cards can wear out, become corrupted, or be accidentally overwritten when experimenting. A full image preserves every partition, installed package, and configuration file exactly as they were, which is ideal when you need to return to a known working state. File-level backups focus on the files that matter most — your scripts, configuration files, and data directories — and are faster and more space-efficient for frequent changes. When you use both, the image handles disaster recovery and rsync handles daily changes. A common misconception is that a single copy is enough. In practice, keep at least two copies: an image stored on a computer or external drive, and incremental backups on another device or network location. Another pitfall is forgetting to back up configuration files; these often live in home directories or /etc and must be included. Example: a weather station project with custom Python scripts, a camera, and cron jobs. An image will restore the full system, but nightly rsync backups of the project folder and config files let you recover recent edits without restoring the whole card. Key takeaway: plan for both catastrophic and incremental loss, and verify backups regularly. How would you prioritize files for a small sensor project?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Combine full images for catastrophic recovery with file-level backups for daily work to cover both failure modes.

content.html:
Core Concept › Why backups matter
Failure modes and strategy

SD cards can fail mechanically, be corrupted by power loss, or be accidentally overwritten. Choose a backup that matches the likely failure: full image for total restore, file-level for ongoing edits.

Full image — when to use
When you want an exact replica to restore the entire system.
File backup — when to use
When you edit code and data frequently and need quick restores.
Common mistake
Relying on a single backup copy or forgetting to include config files in backups.
Key Takeaway

Mix full images and incremental backups, and verify both regularly.

Concrete example: sensor project
Keep a full image weekly. Use nightly rsync for the project folder, camera images, and cron scripts. Store the image on a laptop and the rsync mirror on an external drive or network server.
Checklist to prioritize files
  • Configuration files and system services (e.g., cron entries).
  • Your project scripts and any data directories.
  • Hardware wiring notes and camera images if relevant.
Misconception check
An image alone is not convenient for recovering a single changed script; rsync solves that. Conversely, rsync alone won't help if the OS partition is corrupted.

screens.title: Create a full SD card image
screens.subtitle: Using Raspberry Pi Imager or dd on macOS/Linux

narration.text: Creating a full SD card image captures every sector of the card so you can later write the exact state back to another card. On a desktop, use Raspberry Pi Imager’s Read option to save the card as an image file; this provides a guided UI. On Mac O S or Linux you can use the dd tool for a raw copy. With dd you specify an input device and an output file; it copies all bytes and can include a progress indicator. The visual panel shows the exact dd usage and a short checklist: identify the correct device path, unmount partitions before copying, and confirm the target path before writing. A serious risk with dd is reversing input and output — that can overwrite your computer’s drive. Always double-check device names and, if possible, use a GUI imager if you are unsure. Example: for a working Pi image, save backup. img to your laptop and verify size and checksum. After creating an image, test restore to a spare card and boot the Pi to confirm the process worked. Would you automate image creation or keep it manual for safety?

keyIdea.title: Process
keyIdea.text: Image creation is straightforward but risky: verify device paths, unmount, and test the restored image on a spare card.

content.html:
Process Flow › Create full SD image
Quick steps for imaging
  1. Identify the SD device path on your computer and unmount its partitions.
  2. Copy the entire card to an image file using a GUI imager or dd.
  3. Verify image size and checksum, then store it off the Pi.
  4. Test by writing the image to a spare card and booting the Pi.
Danger note
Be extremely careful with dd. Reversing device paths will overwrite drives. Prefer a guided imager if you are unsure.
Key Takeaway

Imaging is reliable but unforgiving; verify and test restores before relying on an image.

Example commands (visual reference)
# Use Raspberry Pi Imager: select "Read" to save the SD card as an image
# Or on macOS/Linux: raw copy with dd (visual shown for learners)
Imaging checklist
  • Unmount the SD card partitions before copying.
  • Note the device path and double-check it.
  • Store the image on a separate drive and verify it boots.
Common mistake
Trying to image a mounted card or assuming the image is valid without testing it on a spare card.

screens.title: Understanding and using dd safely
screens.subtitle: Low-level copying with care — verify device paths and permissions

narration.text: The dd tool performs a raw, byte-for-byte copy from one device to another. It is powerful because it does not care about filesystems; it copies blocks. That power is also the reason to be cautious. Before using dd, identify the correct device path for the SD card on your computer. On Linux this might be something like the sdX name; on Mac O S it can be diskN. Unmount all partitions of the SD card so the operating system does not interfere. Then run dd to create an image file. After the copy, check the image file size and, if available, a checksum to confirm integrity. A safe workflow includes writing the image to a known spare card and booting the Pi to validate it. A common misconception is that dd is slow because of options; in many cases its throughput depends on block size; using a moderate block size speeds the copy. Another misconception is that dd makes backups incremental — it does not. It always produces a full image. If you want incremental updates, use rsync instead. Would you reserve dd for weekly or occasional full snapshots, and rely on rsync for nightly changes?

keyIdea.title: dd best practice
keyIdea.text: Use dd for full, exact backups only after unmounting and confirming device paths; verify the image by testing a restore.

content.html:
Definition › Using dd safely
What dd does

Dd copies raw blocks from a device to a file or from a file to a device. It ignores filesystem structure and preserves every byte, which makes it suitable for full images.

Safe workflow
  • Unmount the SD card partitions.
  • Confirm the device name with a reliable tool.
  • Run the copy and verify the resulting image.
  • Test by writing to a spare card and booting the Pi.
Critical warning
If you switch input and output, dd will overwrite drives. Always triple-check the device paths before running the command.
Visual code reference
# Example: create an image of the SD card
# sudo dd if=/dev/sdX of=backup.img bs=4M status=progress

# Example: restore the image to a card
# sudo dd if=backup.img of=/dev/sdX bs=4M status=progress
Note: commands shown for visual reference in the lesson. Do not run without adapting device paths.
Misconception
Dd is not an incremental backup. It creates one full image each time and will overwrite target devices if used incorrectly.

narration.text: Rsync is the go-to tool for file-level backups because it copies only what changed and can preserve permissions and timestamps. Use rsync with archive mode to maintain structure, and add compression for network transfers. A typical command backs up a home directory to an external drive or a mounted backup folder. The visual panel shows a practical rsync example and explains the --delete flag, which removes files from the backup that no longer exist on the source to keep both sides synchronized. That option is valuable when you want a mirror, but it can remove files unintentionally if you run rsync against the wrong source. Another common mistake is forgetting to include a trailing slash on the source path, which changes rsync’s behavior about copying the directory itself versus its contents. Example scenario: keep /home/pi/projects mirrored nightly to /mnt/backup/pi_projects with a scheduled job. After running rsync, spot-check files to ensure permissions and recent edits were copied. If you need historical snapshots, combine rsync with dated directories or use a snapshot tool. How would you protect against accidental deletions when using --delete?

keyIdea.title: Rsync principle
keyIdea.text: Rsync copies differences efficiently; use --delete only when you intend to mirror and test runs before automating deletions.

content.html:
Process Flow › File-level backups with rsync
Rsync essentials

Use rsync to copy changed files, preserve permissions, and optionally compress for network transfers. It’s efficient for nightly backups or synchronizing a development folder.

Key options to know
  • -a archive mode to preserve attributes.
  • -v verbose so you can see progress.
  • -z compress over network transfers.
  • --delete remove files from the backup that no longer exist on the source.
Common mistake
Using --delete without testing can remove files unintentionally. Always test with a dry run first.
Example command (visual)
# Back up a home directory to a mounted backup folder
# rsync -avz --delete /home/alex/ /mnt/backup/pi_home/
Tip: the trailing slash on the source copies contents of the directory. Omit it to copy the directory itself.
Protection strategy
Run rsync with --dry-run first to confirm actions. Keep a short history or dated folders to recover unintended deletions.

screens.title: Full image vs. rsync backups
screens.subtitle: When to use each approach and how they complement each other

narration.text: Choosing between a full image and rsync is not an either-or decision; each serves different needs. A full image is a byte-for-byte snapshot of the entire SD card. It’s ideal when you want to recreate the exact system state including installed packages, system-level configuration, and partition layout. Rsync, by contrast, operates at the file level and copies only changed files. It’s faster and uses less space for frequent backups of scripts and data. Use an image when preparing to hand someone an exact replica, performing a one-off migration, or before risky upgrades. Use rsync for nightly or hourly backups of active project folders. A typical plan: keep weekly or monthly full images and daily rsync snapshots. Watch out for the misconception that an image replaces the need for rsync; images are slower to create and restore. Another common mistake is running rsync without preserving permissions or timestamps; that can break scripts or services. Example: a camera project might need frequent image backups for media and periodic full images when system packages change. The core question to decide is: do you need an exact system state, or just your changed files?

keyIdea.title: Comparison
keyIdea.text: Use full images for exact system recovery and rsync for efficient, frequent file backups; combine both for robust recovery.

content.html:
Comparison › Image vs rsync
Full image
Byte-for-byte copy including OS, partitions, and installed packages. Slow to create but simple to restore.
  • Pros: exact replica, simple restore.
  • Cons: large files, not incremental.
  • When: before major changes, migrations, or long-term archival.
Rsync
File-level sync that transfers only changed files. Fast for regular backups and efficient over network links.
  • Pros: incremental, space-efficient, configurable.
  • Cons: not a full system snapshot; requires careful selection of files.
  • When: nightly backups of project folders and data.
Combined approach
Keep periodic full images and daily rsync mirrors. Test restores from both types and log where copies are stored.

screens.title: Automating backups with cron
screens.subtitle: Schedule nightly rsync jobs and keep logs

narration.text: Automation removes human error and makes backups reliable. Use cron to schedule rsync jobs to run at predictable times, for example every night at midnight. Write a small script that calls rsync with the options you trust, logs output to a file, and rotates logs periodically. The script should include a dry-run option you can enable for testing and an explicit check to ensure the destination is mounted before copying. A simple schedule might run a nightly rsync to an attached USB drive and a weekly full image manually created and stored on a laptop. Always include logging: capture rsync output and errors so you can confirm success. Common mistakes include hardcoding device paths that change or not testing the script manually before scheduling. Example: a cron entry that runs the rsync script daily and sends output to a log file. Also consider disk space: add a check that prevents backups if the destination is low on space. Automation is powerful but must include safeguards. How will you verify your automated backups weekly? Automating backups with cron means use cron to schedule tested rsync scripts, include logging and checks for mount points and available space before running.. In practical terms, schedule nightly rsync jobs and keep logs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Automation
keyIdea.text: Use cron to schedule tested rsync scripts, include logging and checks for mount points and available space before running.

content.html:
Process Flow › Automating with cron
Safe automation pattern
  1. Create a small script that runs rsync and writes a timestamped log.
  2. Include checks: ensure destination is mounted and has sufficient space.
  3. Test the script manually, then add it to cron with an explicit schedule.
  4. Monitor logs and test restores weekly.
Pro tip
Use a log rotation policy or dated backup folders so old backups do not fill the destination.
Example cron entry (visual)
# Run backup script every night at midnight
# 0 0 * * * /home/pi/bin/backup_rsync.sh >> /var/log/backup_rsync.log 2>&1
Make the script idempotent and safe: check mounts and return meaningful exit codes for monitoring.
Common mistake
Scheduling without testing or logging leads to silent failures. Always test and monitor logs or alerts.

screens.title: Documenting your project for disaster recovery
screens.subtitle: What to include in a README so rebuilds are repeatable

narration.text: Documentation is the glue that makes backups useful. A good README answers the question: how do I rebuild this project from scratch? Include a brief project description and goals so someone knows the purpose. Add a hardware list with part numbers and wiring notes or photos, because exact parts matter for connectors and power. Describe software dependencies and installation steps so that required packages and versions can be reproduced. Show how to run the project and include startup commands or service setups. Finally, add explicit backup and restore steps: where images and backups are stored, how to restore an image, and how to use the rsync script. A frequent mistake is assuming the user remembers manual tweaks or local credentials. Instead, record special configuration values and where sensitive credentials live, and explain how to recreate them without exposing secrets in the README. Example: include a short section titled ‘Restore steps’ that explains writing an image to a new card and running any post-restore repairs. Key takeaway: documented steps reduce restore time and avoid guesswork about missing dependencies or wiring. Documenting your project for disaster recovery means a readme should list hardware, wiring, dependencies, run steps, and backup/restore instructions to enable reliable rebuilds.. In practical terms, what to include in a readme so rebuilds are repeatable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Documentation
keyIdea.text: A README should list hardware, wiring, dependencies, run steps, and backup/restore instructions to enable reliable rebuilds.

content.html:
Definition › Project documentation
Essential README sections
  • Project description and goals — what problem the project solves.
  • Hardware list — part numbers, power requirements, and connectors.
  • Wiring notes — diagrams or photos, pin mappings for sensors and cameras.
  • Software dependencies — packages and versions, installation commands.
  • Run and restore steps — how to run, where backups live, and how to restore from an image or rsync mirror.
Example: Restore steps (short)
Write the stored backup image to a spare SD card, boot the Pi, then run the post-restore script to re-enable services and update paths.
Why docs matter
Clear docs save hours when restoring. They also help collaborators and future-you understand design choices and required steps.
Common omission
Missing post-restore steps like re-enabling services or regenerating keys often prevent a restored system from working immediately.

screens.title: Hands-on: image + rsync daily backups
screens.subtitle: A practical exercise to create an image, write an rsync script, and schedule it

narration.text: This hands-on activity ties everything together. First, create a full SD image using Raspberry Pi Imager or dd and store it on a separate computer. Verify the file exists and test writing it to a spare card to confirm the backup. Second, write a small rsync script that mirrors your project directory to a USB drive. The script should be explicit about source and destination paths, run rsync with archive mode, and log output to a file. Third, add a cron job to run the script at midnight. Before scheduling, run the script manually and inspect the log to confirm success. Keep a short verification checklist: confirm mount, run rsync with --dry-run, check logs, and rotate or remove older backups as needed. A common mistake is trusting the cron job without checking logs for errors; check logs and test restores from both the image and rsync copy. This exercise helps you practice the important habit: create an image for total restore and use rsync for day-to-day changes so you can recover recent work quickly. Hands-on: image + rsync daily backups means create an image, build a tested rsync script, and automate with cron while keeping verification and logs.. In practical terms, a practical exercise to create an image, write an rsync script, and schedule it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Activity
keyIdea.text: Create an image, build a tested rsync script, and automate with cron while keeping verification and logs.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity › Image + rsync
Step 1 — Create and verify image
Save the image to your laptop, check file size and checksum, and write to a spare card to boot and confirm.
Step 2 — rsync script
#!/bin/sh
# backup_rsync.sh
# rsync -avz --delete /home/pi/projects/ /mnt/backup/pi_projects/
Make the script check that /mnt/backup is mounted and write logs with timestamps.
Step 3 — Schedule and verify
Add a cron entry for midnight, then inspect the resulting log after the first run. Perform a restore from both the image and the rsync copy to confirm completeness.
Verification checklist
  • Destination mounted and writable.
  • Rsync dry-run succeeds.
  • Log file contains success lines and no errors.
  • Restore test boots and runs as expected.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: These three key concepts wrap up the chapter. First, full SD card images capture the entire system and are essential for complete recovery, but they are large and not incremental. Second, rsync provides efficient, incremental file-level backups and can mirror directories with the --delete option when used carefully. Third, documentation completes the recovery story: a clear README listing hardware, wiring, dependencies, and restore steps makes backups usable. Keep these ideas together: images for disaster recovery, rsync for daily work, and readable documentation so restores are predictable. Verify backups by testing restores and monitoring logs so you don’t discover a failed backup during a real emergency. Which concept will you apply first to your current Raspberry Pi project? Key Concepts means images + rsync + documentation form a complete, testable recovery plan.. In practical terms, what to remember from this chapter. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Images + rsync + documentation form a complete, testable recovery plan.

content.html:
Summary › Key Concepts
Full SD images
Create complete, bootable snapshots for disaster recovery.
File-level rsync
Efficient incremental backups; use --delete only with care.
Documentation
A README with parts, wiring, install, and restore steps makes backups useful.
Final takeaway

Test your backups and keep at least two copies in different locations to ensure recoverability.

screens.title: Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Commands, options, and practices to use right away

narration.text: Keep a short reference for the commands and practices you’ll use daily. Remember that dd creates full images and requires careful device selection and unmounting. Rsync with archive and compression is your friend for incremental backups, and the --delete option makes a mirror but needs testing. Automate with cron but ensure scripts check mounts and log their output. Finally, write a concise README with hardware, wiring, and restore steps so your backups are actionable. Having a one-page checklist that lists imaging steps, an rsync script path, and the restore procedure will save time in an emergency. After a backup routine is in place, test a restore at least once to confirm you can recover and that the README steps are complete. What would you include on your one-page recovery checklist?

keyIdea.title: Quick reference
keyIdea.text: Use dd for full images, rsync for incremental backups, automate safely, and keep a one-page recovery checklist.

content.html:
What to Remember › Quick Reference
Imaging
Create an image, verify, and test on a spare card.
Rsync
Use -avz, test with --dry-run, and be careful with --delete.
Automation
Script checks, log output, schedule with cron, and monitor logs.
One-line checklist

Image weekly, rsync nightly, keep two copies, test restore monthly, and include restore steps in README.
